title: The art of building billion-dollar businesses
author: Sharran Srivatsaa
summary: Sharran Srivatsaa, a serial founder now building Acquisition.com, lays out four steps he would follow to build a billion-dollar company again: sales, operations, people and partnerships, in that order. He argues that founders must sell before they know product-market fit, and that a CEO should learn sales and marketing rather than delegate them, illustrating the point with the story of Tesla's uncalled test-drive leads. Operations come only after the offer and sales process are proven, because systems built too early simply make a broken process more efficient, while systems built too late create the "curse of capability" in which the founder becomes the bottleneck. On people, he insists that hiring is a learnable skill and that a failed hire is a reason to hire better, not to stop delegating. Partnerships then become possible because nobody partners with potential, only with demonstrated results, as in Real's path to acquiring RE/MAX. He closes with a ladder of constraints by revenue stage and urges leaders to find the real constraint before working on the wrong problem.
points: A founder has to sell before product-market fit is known, which means launching the best version available now and iterating, because early promises can only be tested by selling.
The "curse of capability" describes how the better a leader is at something, the more the business depends on them, so any task that works and recurs should become a documented system.
A weak offer does not need better systems or sales; it needs to be killed, because good operations only make a bad offer fail more efficiently.

A failed hire signals a gap in the leader's hiring skill, and building a hiring funnel with job descriptions written around real pain points and standing questions about logistics fixes the process rather than abandoning delegation.
The binding constraint changes with each revenue stage, so leaders should diagnose the actual constraint before spending effort on a problem that is not holding the business back.
quotes: Early sales have to be sales-led. This means you’re making promises the product hasn’t earned just yet.
This is why sales and marketing are the first two things a CEO should actually learn, not delegate.
If you build operations before proving the offer and sales process work, you’re just making a broken process more efficient.
The better you are at something, the more the business relies on you being there to run. Until eventually you’re not valuable… you’re the bottleneck.
A weak offer doesn’t need a better sales process or system, it needs to be killed.
It just means you hired the wrong person, and that’s a skill problem on your end. It’s not a sign to stop delegating.
Nobody partners with you for your potential. They partner with you for what you’ve already shown you can do.
But most businesses are working hard on a problem that isn’t actually the one holding them back.
